---
title: "The Drunkard Who Maps the City"
---

> **The big question of this module.** What does a network look like to a walker who has no idea where they are going?

## A Walker With No Plan

Suppose you walk in a city. You are drunk and your feet have no idea where to go. You just take a step wherever your feet take you. At every intersection, you make a random decision and take a step. This is the core idea of a random walk.

You are not trying to get anywhere, and that is exactly the point. You have no map, no destination, no memory of the street you came from. Every decision you make is a coin flip among the streets in front of you.

While your feet are taking you to a random street, after making many steps and looking back, you will realize that you have been to certain places more frequently than others. If you were to map the frequency of your visits to each street, you will end up with a distribution that tells you about salient structure of the street network. The drunkard, who understood nothing, has produced a measurement.

Here is that measurement being made, on ten nodes. Take the first few steps one
at a time to see the rule, then let the tally run: the bars are the walker's own
record of where it has been.

```{=html}
<style>
/* --------------------------------------------------------------------------
   The walker's tally — only the rules this one stage needs. The paper, the
   panels, the buttons, the ink and the motion all come from assets/anim.css;

   -------------------------------------------------------------------------- */

  font-family: var(--_hand);

/* The two states an edge takes while the walker is choosing. */

#rw-degree .rw-edge-hot { stroke: var(--_amber); stroke-width: 4.6; }

/* The walker is a ring round the node it is standing on, not a disc, so the
   node's own number still reads through it. */
#rw-degree .rw-glow { fill: var(--_amber); fill-opacity: 0.16; stroke: none; }
#rw-degree .rw-ring { fill: none; stroke: var(--_amber); stroke-width: 3.2; }

/* The start picker of the last scene. Dead until that scene turns it on, so
   the earlier scenes cannot be clicked out from under themselves. */
#rw-degree .rw-hit { fill: transparent; pointer-events: none; }
#rw-degree .rw-pick .rw-hit { pointer-events: auto; cursor: pointer; }
#rw-degree .rw-pick .rw-hit:hover { fill: var(--_accent); fill-opacity: 0.2; }

/* Bars for walkers two and three; walker one uses the kit's .anim-accent-fill. */
#rw-degree .rw-bar-b { fill: var(--_amber); }
#rw-degree .rw-bar-c { fill: var(--_ink-faint); }

<script>
/* The walker's tally. Markup above, scenes below, and nothing in between: the
   paper, the pen, the motion and the sequencer all come from assets/anim.css +
   assets/anim.js, and everything a scene calls arrives on `ctx`. The kit is
   loaded after this file, hence the animReady queue. */
(window.animReady = window.animReady || []).push(function () {

  /* ---------------------------------------------------------------- data ---
     Every number below was computed once, offline, from one fixed seed, and
     pasted in. Nothing here runs a graph algorithm or draws a random number at
     page load, so every reader watches the identical walk and sees exactly the
     numbers this caption claims.

     The network is the one the rest of this module uses: 10 nodes, 13 edges,
     degrees (2,4,3,4,4,3,2,1,2,1). So 2m = 26 and
       k/2m = (.077, .154, .115, .154, .154, .115, .077, .038, .077, .038).
     It is connected and it contains triangles, so the walk is neither
     reducible nor periodic and a stationary distribution exists.
     ------------------------------------------------------------------------ */
  const NODE = [[38,70],[100,34],[166,48],[54,134],[126,104],[92,186],[158,162],[200,22],[196,118],[200,190]];
  const EDGE = [[0,1],[0,3],[1,2],[1,3],[1,4],[2,4],[2,7],[3,4],[3,5],[4,5],[5,6],[6,8],[8,9]];
  const DEG  = [2,4,3,4,4,3,2,1,2,1];
  const ADJ  = [[1,3],[0,2,3,4],[1,4,7],[0,1,4,5],[1,2,3,5],[3,4,6],[5,8],[2],[6,9],[8]];
  const TWO_M = 26;
  const PI = DEG.map((k) => k / TWO_M);

  /* One recorded walk, started at node 0. Each character is a node: SEQ[0] is
     the start and SEQ[t] is where the walker stands after t steps. 600 steps,
     replayed here one at a time. */
  const SEQ =
    "010141356898986865412143530135431345689898689898653568686868686865689898689865410301272421034303565456530354310303541353" +
    "427272454312727241421012721035456898653531310356545689868654345301453434212424130303131272135353430313013010342103145456" +
    "541035654303013568653124143568686565689868689865412724241431456568653012421434541303568989898989898654142724343535427242" +
    "721214568989868689898989865431412435414243456541353030143014272143453124313135310354127245421245343014565435454312134356" +
    "898653121242431342430310134342410121242727241272721303568989865421301272453568986545454568654210141245689868989868989898" +
    "6";

  /* The same walk carried past step 600 and tallied at nine checkpoints. Each
     row is [steps, share of all visits per node in parts per thousand, the node
     the walker is standing on]. Counting SEQ character by character reproduces
     the first row exactly, so the hand-played part and the pasted part meet
     without a seam. */
  const LADDER = [
    [   600, [62,123,100,143,148,125,98,30,113,58], 6],
    [  1000, [66,143,124,153,154,112,80,44, 83,42], 2],
    [  1700, [66,146,120,146,150,115,82,45, 86,44], 2],
    [  3000, [68,145,116,152,151,116,80,43, 85,46], 9],
    [  5200, [78,152,112,153,149,114,80,38, 82,42], 2],
    [  9000, [73,145,115,151,153,118,81,40, 82,42], 4],
    [ 16000, [74,147,113,154,153,119,79,38, 81,43], 8],
    [ 28000, [73,152,118,152,153,117,78,41, 77,39], 7],
    [ 50000, [75,152,117,153,154,117,78,39, 77,39], 3]
  ];

  /* Three more recorded walks, from three deliberately unalike nodes: the leaf
     7, the hub 1, and the leaf 9 at the far end of the tail. Same tally, taken
     at 6, 30, 200, 2000 and 20000 steps. */
  const TRIO_T = [6, 30, 200, 2000, 20000];
  const TRIO_START = [7, 1, 9];
  const TRIO = [
    [[0,143,143,143,286,143,0,143,0,0],[32,226,226,97,258,32,0,129,0,0],[95,159,114,174,199,124,60,55,20,0],[83,158,114,170,159,114,70,44,59,27],[76,157,120,155,154,115,76,41,72,35]],
    [[0,143,0,143,429,286,0,0,0,0],[65,258,32,258,258,129,0,0,0,0],[55,159,90,179,179,154,75,10,65,35],[60,161,128,149,179,114,68,37,69,34],[76,152,116,152,154,117,78,40,77,38]],
    [[0,0,143,0,286,143,143,0,143,143],[0,129,226,161,194,129,32,65,32,32],[75,174,124,129,144,119,90,25,80,40],[78,151,121,146,139,115,84,39,83,42],[76,154,113,157,153,118,77,37,77,39]]
  ];

  /* One recorded walk per possible starting node, for the scene the reader
     drives. SHORT[s] is its first 20 steps written out node by node; MID[s] and
     FIN[s] are that same walk's tally after 300 and after 20000 steps, again in
     parts per thousand. */
  const SHORT = ["031413542721427242413","121212134303568653542","242121031213013142424","356545421427272143013","456568689898686868989","568989865689868689898","653124565356898656898","727245656865653142413","865314245314213545427","986865653012131245454"];
  const MID = [[56,126,166,130,133,113,80,90,73,33],[60,166,130,133,166,123,93,33,70,27],[80,186,176,150,163,113,47,60,20,7],[70,166,96,126,140,136,120,23,96,27],[73,150,140,130,136,100,86,63,86,37],[43,106,83,133,176,120,110,20,136,73],[63,133,113,126,143,116,90,40,110,66],[70,146,126,176,173,116,66,50,53,23],[113,163,83,206,176,120,47,20,47,27],[56,130,110,146,166,126,86,33,96,50]];
  const FIN = [[74,153,115,152,153,118,79,38,78,39],[75,151,113,151,153,117,83,37,81,39],[79,154,112,157,152,121,80,36,74,36],[76,157,118,153,158,115,75,38,74,37],[81,153,113,161,151,112,73,38,77,40],[76,153,110,158,156,119,78,35,76,38],[77,157,112,153,152,111,76,38,81,42],[76,153,117,157,160,117,75,39,71,34],[76,153,117,156,159,120,77,37,72,34],[75,155,119,152,159,116,75,38,74,37]];

  const SLOW = 7;              /* steps of SEQ played out one at a time */
  const KEY = ["var(--_accent)", "var(--_amber)", "var(--_ink-faint)"];

  /* ------------------------------------------------------------- geometry --- */
  const GX = (i) => 46 + 21 * i;   /* centre of node i's bar group */
  const YB = 132;                  /* the baseline */
  const PLOT = 110;                /* full height of the plot */
  /* The tally starts absurd — one visit, all of it at the start node — so the
     top of the scale steps down through these as it settles. From about step 30
     on it is pinned at 20 % and never moves again. */
  const AXIS = [1, 0.6, 0.4, 0.3, 0.25, 0.2];
  const axisFor = (mx) => {
    let a = AXIS[0];
    for (let i = 0; i < AXIS.length; i++) if (AXIS[i] >= mx + 0.004) a = AXIS[i];
    return a;
  };
  const pct = (a) => Math.round(a * 100) + "%";
  const f3 = (x) => x.toFixed(3);
  const f2 = (x) => x.toFixed(2).replace(/^0/, "");
  const thou = (n) => n.toLocaleString("en-US");
  const swatch = (j) => '<span style="color:' + KEY[j] + '">&#9632;</span>';

  /* --------------------------------------------------------------- scenes --- */
  const scenes = [
    {
      label: "One step: pick a neighbour",
      note: "The whole rule, seven steps of it. Standing on a node, the walker looks at that node's neighbours and takes one at random — every one of them equally likely. Each landing raises that node's bar by one.",
      async run(ctx) {
        ctx.build();
        const c = ctx.say("the rule");
        const line = ctx.el("div", "anim-tally", "<span>standing on</span><b>0</b>");
        const odds = ctx.el("div", "anim-caption", "");
        c.appendChild(line);
        c.appendChild(odds);

        if (ctx.fast()) {
          ctx.prefix(SEQ.slice(0, SLOW + 1));
          line.querySelector("b").textContent = SEQ[SLOW];
          odds.textContent = "landed on " + SEQ[SLOW] + " — its bar goes up by one";
          return;
        }

        ctx.visit(0, false);
        await ctx.sleep(900);
        for (let t = 1; t <= SLOW; t++) {
          const from = +SEQ[t - 1], to = +SEQ[t];
          line.querySelector("b").textContent = String(from);
          odds.textContent = "neighbours of " + from + ": " + ADJ[from].join(", ") +
            " — each with chance 1/" + DEG[from];
          ctx.offer(from);
          await ctx.sleep(680);
          ctx.take(from, to);
          ctx.visit(to, true);
          /* The card follows the walker, so it never reads as standing on the
             node it has just left. */
          line.querySelector("b").textContent = String(to);
          odds.textContent = "landed on " + to + " — its bar goes up by one";
          await ctx.sleep(540);
          if (t === 2) {
            c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-quote anim-fade",
              "step 2 went straight back where step 1 came from — the walker keeps no memory of the street it just used"));
          }
        }
        ctx.cool();
        await ctx.sleep(1600);
      }
    },
    {
      label: "Let it run",
      note: "Now let it go. Six hundred steps arrive one at a time and the bars stay lumpy: nodes 0 and 8 have the same degree, yet at step 600 node 8 has been visited nearly twice as often. Then the counter runs to fifty thousand, and the bars stop moving.",
      async run(ctx) {
        const c = ctx.say("let it run");
        const big = ctx.el("div", "anim-big", "0");
        c.appendChild(big);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption", "steps taken"));
        const verdict = ctx.el("div", "anim-tally anim-fade");
        verdict.style.visibility = "hidden";
        c.appendChild(verdict);
        const last = LADDER[LADDER.length - 1];

        if (ctx.fast()) {
          ctx.snapshot(last);
          big.textContent = thou(last[0]);
          verdict.innerHTML = "<span>they stopped moving.</span><b>at what?</b>";
          verdict.style.visibility = "visible";
          return;
        }

        /* SEQ replayed at a rising pace — single steps first, so one bar can
           still be seen going up, then handfuls. */
        let t = SLOW;
        while (t < 600) {
          const chunk = t < 34 ? 1 : t < 100 ? 3 : t < 260 ? 8 : 20;
          for (let k = 0; k < chunk && t < 600; k++) { t++; ctx.visit(+SEQ[t], true); }
          big.textContent = thou(t);
          await ctx.sleep(1);
        }
        verdict.innerHTML = "<span>600 steps in</span><b>still lumpy</b>";
        verdict.style.visibility = "visible";
        await ctx.sleep(1600);

        for (let i = 1; i < LADDER.length; i++) {
          ctx.snapshot(LADDER[i]);
          big.textContent = thou(LADDER[i][0]);
          await ctx.sleep(540);
        }
        verdict.innerHTML = "<span>they stopped moving.</span><b>at what?</b>";
        await ctx.sleep(2400);
      }
    },
    {
      label: "The bars are the degrees",
      note: "Freeze it, and lay a dashed marker across each bar at k over 2m — that node's degree divided by the 26 edge endpoints in the network. Every bar is sitting on its marker. The bottom row of the chart is the answer.",
      async run(ctx) {
        const c = ctx.say("what the bars settled on");
        ctx.marks(true);
        if (!ctx.fast()) await ctx.sleep(1300);
        ctx.degrees(true);
        if (!ctx.fast()) await ctx.sleep(1300);

        [["node 1, k = 4", "0.154 &rarr; 0.152"],
         ["node 7, k = 1", "0.038 &rarr; 0.039"]].forEach((row, i) => {
          const t = ctx.el("div", "anim-tally anim-fade",
            "<span>" + row[0] + "</span><b>" + row[1] + "</b>");
          t.style.animationDelay = ctx.fast() ? "0s" : (i * 0.6) + "s";
          c.appendChild(t);
        });
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption",
          "k/2m predicted &rarr; share measured over 50,000 steps"));
        if (!ctx.fast()) await ctx.sleep(2000);

        const q = ctx.el("div", "anim-quote anim-fade",
          "the walker&rsquo;s long-run share of time at a node is just that node&rsquo;s degree over the total");
        c.appendChild(q);
        await ctx.sleep(3200);
      }
    },
    {
      label: "It forgets where it started",
      note: "Three walkers now, from a leaf, from the hub, and from the leaf at the far end of the tail. Six steps in, the three tallies have nothing in common. Twenty thousand steps in they are the same picture — and it is the one the markers already predicted.",
      async run(ctx) {
        const c = ctx.say("three walkers, three starting nodes");
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption",
          "started at &nbsp;" + swatch(0) + " 7 &nbsp; " + swatch(1) + " 1 &nbsp; " +
          swatch(2) + " 9"));
        const big = ctx.el("div", "anim-big", "6");
        c.appendChild(big);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption", "steps taken, each of the three"));
        const verdict = ctx.el("div", "anim-tally anim-fade");
        verdict.style.visibility = "hidden";
        c.appendChild(verdict);

        ctx.starts(TRIO_START);
        const last = TRIO_T.length - 1;

        if (ctx.fast()) {
          ctx.trio(last);
          big.textContent = thou(TRIO_T[last]);
          verdict.innerHTML = "<span>same profile</span><b>start erased</b>";
          verdict.style.visibility = "visible";
          return;
        }

        for (let i = 0; i < TRIO_T.length; i++) {
          ctx.trio(i);
          big.textContent = thou(TRIO_T[i]);
          if (i === 0) {
            verdict.innerHTML = "<span>six steps in</span><b>nothing in common</b>";
            verdict.style.visibility = "visible";
          }
          await ctx.sleep(i === 0 ? 2400 : 1600);
        }
        verdict.innerHTML = "<span>same profile</span><b>start erased</b>";
        await ctx.sleep(3200);
      }
    },
    {
      label: "Now you choose the start",
      note: "Click any node in the network to drop the walker there and run it again. Twenty steps in, the tally is all about where you put it. Twenty thousand steps in it is back on the markers — every time, from every node.",
      async run(ctx) {
        const c = ctx.say("you choose where it starts");
        const big = ctx.el("div", "anim-big", "&mdash;");
        c.appendChild(big);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption", "steps taken"));
        const hint = ctx.el("div", "anim-tally", "<span>click any node</span><b>&#9758;</b>");
        c.appendChild(hint);
        const verdict = ctx.el("div", "anim-tally anim-fade");
        verdict.style.visibility = "hidden";
        c.appendChild(verdict);

        const show = (n, txt) => {
          big.innerHTML = n;
          if (txt) { verdict.innerHTML = txt; verdict.style.visibility = "visible"; }
        };

        const tour = [9, 7, 4];
        let rounds = 0;
        let queued = null;

        /* Waiting, in slices, so a click gets an answer inside a tenth of a
           second instead of at the end of whatever pause is running. Returns
           false once this run has been superseded. */
        async function nap(ms, id) {
          for (let left = ms; left > 0; left -= 110) {
            await ctx.sleep(Math.min(110, left));
            if (id !== ctx.runId()) return false;
          }
          return true;
        }

        /* One run from node s: twenty steps played out on the network, then the
           same recorded walk's tally at 300 and at 20000 steps. */
        async function runFrom(s, instant) {
          const id = ctx.newRun();
          ctx.reset();
          hint.querySelector("b").textContent = "start = " + s;
          show("0", "<span>starting at " + s + "</span><b>&hellip;</b>");
          const w = SHORT[s];
          if (!instant) {
            for (let t = 0; t <= 20; t++) {
              ctx.visit(+w[t], t > 0);
              show(String(t));
              if (!await nap(t < 6 ? 280 : 130, id)) return;
            }
            show("20", "<span>20 steps</span><b>nowhere near</b>");
            if (!await nap(1600, id)) return;
          }
          ctx.snapshot([300, MID[s], -1]);
          show(thou(300));
          if (!instant && !await nap(950, id)) return;
          ctx.snapshot([20000, FIN[s], -1]);
          show(thou(20000), "<span>20,000 steps</span><b>on the markers</b>");
          if (!instant) await nap(2400, id);
        }

        /* The one loop that ever starts a run, so the reader's node cannot be
           stolen back by the tour. */
        let looping = false;
        async function pump() {
          if (looping) return;
          looping = true;
          try {
            while (rounds < tour.length || queued !== null) {
              let s;
              if (queued !== null) { s = queued; queued = null; }
              else { s = tour[rounds]; rounds++; }
              await runFrom(s, false);
            }
          } finally { looping = false; }
        }

        /* A click files a request and cancels whatever is in flight. A reader
           who asked for no motion gets the finished tally in one shot instead. */
        ctx.pickable(function (n) {
          if (ctx.reduced) { runFrom(n, true).catch(function () {}); return; }
          ctx.resume();
          queued = n;
          rounds = 0;
          ctx.newRun();
          pump().catch(function () {});
        });

        if (ctx.fast()) {
          await runFrom(9, true);
          return;
        }
        await pump();
      }
    }
  ];

  mountScenes(document.getElementById("rw-degree"), scenes, {
    stepsLabel: "Random-walk steps",

    /* The two things only this animation has: a network the walker moves on and
       a tally chart every scene writes into. Both are built once, in scene 1,
       and only mutated afterwards — so jumping to a step still lands on a
       drawing, because the kit fast-forwards the earlier scenes first. */
    helpers(ctx) {
      const net = ctx.$("[data-rw-net]");
      const bars = ctx.$("[data-rw-bars]");
      const side = ctx.$("[data-rw-say]");
      const S = { run: 0 };

      /* Two index tables, not algorithms: which edges touch a node, and which
         edge joins a given pair. */
      const INC = NODE.map(() => []);
      EDGE.forEach((e, i) => { INC[e[0]].push(i); INC[e[1]].push(i); });
      const EIDX = {};
      EDGE.forEach((e, i) => { EIDX[e[0] + "-" + e[1]] = i; EIDX[e[1] + "-" + e[0]] = i; });

      /* ---------------------------------------------------------- the build */
      function build() {
        net.textContent = "";
        bars.textContent = "";
        S.count = NODE.map(() => 0);
        S.total = 0;
        S.rows = null;
        S.mode = "one";
        S.cand = [];
        S.hot = -1;
        S.onPick = null;
        const slow = !ctx.fast();

        /* ---- the network ---- */
        const svg = ctx.svgRoot("0 0 220 212");
        const g = () => svg.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("g"));
        const gEdge = g(), gTok = g(), gNode = g(), gHit = g();

        S.edges = EDGE.map((e, i) => {
          const a = NODE[e[0]], b = NODE[e[1]];
          const p = ctx.svgEl("line", {
            x1: a[0], y1: a[1], x2: b[0], y2: b[1],
            "class": "anim-edge" + (slow ? " anim-draw" : "")
          });
          if (slow) {
            p.style.setProperty("--dash", Math.ceil(Math.hypot(a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1])) + 2);
            p.style.animationDelay = (0.15 + i * 0.06) + "s";
          }
          return gEdge.appendChild(p);
        });

        S.startG = gTok.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("g"));
        const tok = ctx.svgEl("g", { "class": "anim-glide" });
        tok.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("circle", { r: 15, "class": "rw-glow" }));
        tok.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("circle", { r: 15, "class": "rw-ring" }));
        tok.style.opacity = 0;
        gTok.appendChild(tok);
        S.token = tok;
        S.svg = svg;

        NODE.forEach((q, i) => {
          const h = ctx.svgEl("g", { "class": slow ? "anim-fade" : null });
          if (slow) h.style.animationDelay = (0.9 + i * 0.05) + "s";
          h.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("circle", { cx: q[0], cy: q[1], r: 10, "class": "anim-node" }));
          const lb = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: q[0], y: q[1], "class": "rw-nlabel" });
          lb.textContent = String(i);
          h.appendChild(lb);
          gNode.appendChild(h);

          const hit = ctx.svgEl("circle", { cx: q[0], cy: q[1], r: 17, "class": "rw-hit" });
          hit.addEventListener("click", function () { if (S.onPick) S.onPick(i); });
          gHit.appendChild(hit);
        });

        net.appendChild(svg);
        net.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption",
          "ten nodes, thirteen edges &mdash; the network this module keeps coming back to"));

        /* ---- the tally ---- */
        S.read = ctx.el("div", "anim-readout anim-readout--tight",
          '<span>steps <b data-t>0</b></span>' +
          '<span>node 1 <b data-r1>&mdash;</b></span>' +
          '<span>node 7 <b data-r7>&mdash;</b></span>');
        bars.appendChild(S.read);
        S.outT = S.read.querySelector("[data-t]");
        S.out1 = S.read.querySelector("[data-r1]");
        S.out7 = S.read.querySelector("[data-r7]");

        const bsvg = ctx.svgRoot("0 0 250 168");
        const bg = () => bsvg.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("g"));
        const gBar = bg(), gMark = bg(), gAx = bg();

        S.bar = [0, 1, 2].map((k) => NODE.map((_, i) =>
          gBar.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("rect", {
            x: GX(i) - 7, y: YB, width: 14, height: 0,
            "class": k === 0 ? "anim-accent-fill" : k === 1 ? "rw-bar-b" : "rw-bar-c"
          }))));

        S.mark = NODE.map((_, i) => {
          const l = ctx.svgEl("line",
            { x1: GX(i) - 11, x2: GX(i) + 11, y1: YB, y2: YB, "class": "anim-marker" });
          l.style.opacity = 0;
          return gMark.appendChild(l);
        });

        gAx.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("line",
          { x1: 34, y1: YB, x2: 246, y2: YB, "class": "anim-axis" }));
        S.top = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: 30, y: YB - PLOT + 4, "class": "rw-tick rw-end" });
        gAx.appendChild(S.top);
        const zero = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: 30, y: YB + 4, "class": "rw-tick rw-end" });
        zero.textContent = "0";
        gAx.appendChild(zero);

        const rowLab = (y, txt) => {
          const t = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: 30, y: y, "class": "rw-tick rw-end rw-dim" });
          t.textContent = txt;
          return gAx.appendChild(t);
        };
        rowLab(YB + 15, "node");
        S.deg = [rowLab(YB + 29, "k")];
        NODE.forEach((_, i) => {
          const n = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: GX(i), y: YB + 15, "class": "rw-tick" });
          n.textContent = String(i);
          gAx.appendChild(n);
          const d = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: GX(i), y: YB + 29, "class": "rw-tick rw-dim" });
          d.textContent = String(DEG[i]);
          gAx.appendChild(d);
          S.deg.push(d);
        });
        S.deg.forEach((d) => { d.style.opacity = 0; });

        bars.appendChild(bsvg);
        bars.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption",
          "bar = share of every visit so far. One walk on the network at left, recorded once with a fixed seed, so this is the same walk for every reader."));
        redraw();
      }

      /* Bars, markers and the top of the scale, from whatever S is holding. */
      function redraw() {
        const rows = S.rows ||
          [S.total ? S.count.map((c) => c / S.total) : S.count.map(() => 0)];
        let mx = 0;
        rows.forEach((r) => r.forEach((v) => { if (v > mx) mx = v; }));
        /* An empty chart shows the scale the first single visit will need. */
        const axis = (!S.rows && !S.total) ? AXIS[0] : axisFor(Math.max(mx, PI[1]));
        S.top.textContent = pct(axis);
        const h = (v) => Math.max(0, (v / axis) * PLOT);

        for (let k = 0; k < 3; k++) {
          const r = rows[k] || null;
          const one = S.mode === "one";
          S.bar[k].forEach((rect, i) => {
            rect.setAttribute("x", one ? GX(i) - 7 : GX(i) - 9.5 + k * 6.5);
            rect.setAttribute("width", one ? 14 : 6);
            const v = (r && !(one && k)) ? h(r[i]) : 0;
            rect.setAttribute("y", YB - v);
            rect.setAttribute("height", v);
          });
        }
        S.mark.forEach((l, i) => {
          const y = YB - h(PI[i]);
          l.setAttribute("y1", y);
          l.setAttribute("y2", y);
        });
      }

      function say(title) {
        side.textContent = "";
        const c = ctx.el("div", "anim-panel anim-pop");
        if (title) c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption", title));
        side.appendChild(c);
        return c;
      }

      /* ----------------------------------------------------------- the walk */
      function place(n, glide) {
        S.token.style.opacity = 1;
        if (!glide) S.token.classList.remove("anim-glide");
        S.token.style.transform = "translate(" + NODE[n][0] + "px," + NODE[n][1] + "px)";
        if (!glide) {
          S.token.getBoundingClientRect();      /* commit before re-arming */
          S.token.classList.add("anim-glide");
        }
      }

      function readout(t, row) {
        S.outT.textContent = thou(t);
        S.out1.textContent = f3(row[1]);
        S.out7.textContent = f3(row[7]);
      }

      /* One landing: the walker stands on n, and n's bar goes up by one. */
      function visit(n, glide) {
        place(n, glide);
        S.count[n] += 1;
        S.total += 1;
        S.rows = null;
        S.mode = "one";
        readout(S.total - 1, S.count.map((c) => c / S.total));
        redraw();
      }

      /* The neighbours the walker is about to choose between, then the one it
         took. */
      function offer(from) {
        cool();
        S.cand = INC[from];
        S.cand.forEach((e) => S.edges[e].setAttribute("class", "anim-edge rw-edge-cand"));
      }
      function take(from, to) {
        cool();
        S.hot = EIDX[from + "-" + to];
        S.edges[S.hot].setAttribute("class", "anim-edge rw-edge-hot");
      }
      function cool() {
        S.cand.forEach((e) => S.edges[e].setAttribute("class", "anim-edge"));
        if (S.hot >= 0) S.edges[S.hot].setAttribute("class", "anim-edge");
        S.cand = [];
        S.hot = -1;
      }

      /* ------------------------------------------------------- the pastings */
      /* [steps, parts-per-thousand row, node the walker is on, or -1 for "not
         claiming a position"]. */
      function snapshot(row) {
        cool();
        S.mode = "one";
        S.rows = [row[1].map((v) => v / 1000)];
        S.total = row[0] + 1;
        S.count = S.rows[0].map((v) => v * S.total);
        if (row[2] >= 0) place(row[2], true); else S.token.style.opacity = 0;
        readout(row[0], S.rows[0]);
        redraw();
      }

      const triple = (i, k) => TRIO.map((w, j) =>
        '<span style="color:' + KEY[j] + '">' + f2(w[k][i] / 1000) + "</span>").join("/");

      function trio(k) {
        cool();
        S.mode = "three";
        S.rows = TRIO.map((w) => w[k].map((v) => v / 1000));
        S.token.style.opacity = 0;
        S.outT.textContent = thou(TRIO_T[k]);
        S.out1.innerHTML = triple(1, k);
        S.out7.innerHTML = triple(7, k);
        redraw();
      }

      /* A ring in each walker's own colour on the node it started from. */
      function starts(list) {
        S.startG.textContent = "";
        list.forEach((n, j) => {
          S.startG.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("circle", {
            cx: NODE[n][0], cy: NODE[n][1], r: 15,
            "class": "rw-ring", style: "stroke:" + KEY[j]
          }));
        });
      }

      function marks(on) { S.mark.forEach((l) => { l.style.opacity = on ? 1 : 0; }); }
      function degrees(on) { S.deg.forEach((d) => { d.style.opacity = on ? 1 : 0; }); }

      function reset() {
        S.startG.textContent = "";
        S.count = NODE.map(() => 0);
        S.total = 0;
        S.rows = null;
        S.mode = "one";
        S.token.style.opacity = 0;
        cool();
        readout(0, S.count);
        redraw();
      }

      function pickable(fn) {
        S.onPick = fn;
        S.svg.classList.add("rw-pick");
      }

      /* S is filled by build(), i.e. after helpers() has already run, so
         everything reaching into it has to be a function — the kit copies these
         onto ctx by value at mount time. */
      return {
        build: build, say: say, visit: visit, offer: offer, take: take, cool: cool,
        snapshot: snapshot, trio: trio, starts: starts, marks: marks,
        degrees: degrees, reset: reset, pickable: pickable,
        newRun: function () { return ++S.run; },
        runId: function () { return S.run; },
        /* Skipping or reading without motion: lay down a recorded prefix with
           no animation at all. */
        prefix: function (str) {
          for (let t = 0; t < str.length; t++) visit(+str[t], true);
        }
      };
    }
  });
});
</script>
```

The bars were not decoration. Two things happened in that widget, and the rest
of this module is spent earning both: the tally settled onto the degrees, and it
settled onto the *same* degrees no matter where the walk began.

::: {.column-margin}
Random walks are not a toy. Your Netflix session is one: you click a movie, then a recommended movie, then another. So is a Wikipedia binge from "Coffee" to "Brazil" to "Soccer". So is a day of stock prices. In each case the object being walked on is a network, and the walk is what reveals it.
:::

Written out, the rule you just watched is:

1. Start at a node $i$
2. Randomly choose an edge to traverse to a neighbor node $j$
3. Repeat step 2 until you have taken $T$ steps

::: {.column-margin}
In directed networks, a random walker can only move along the edge direction, and it can be that the random walker is stuck in a so-called "dead end" that does not have any outgoing edges.
:::

## Amida-kuji: A Ladder Decides Your Fate

::: {.callout-note title="Ladder Lottery"}

Ladder Lottery is a fun East Asian game, also known as "鬼腳圖" (Guijiaotu) in Chinese, "阿弥陀籤" (Amida-kuji) in Japanese, "사다리타기" (Sadaritagi) in Korean, and "Ladder Lottery" in English. The game is played as follows:

1. A player is given a board with a set of vertical lines.
2. The player chooses a line and starts to move along the line.
3. When hitting a horizontal line, the player must move along the horizontal line and then continue to move along the next vertical line.
4. The player wins if the player can hit a marked line at the bottom of the board.
5. You cannot see the horizontal lines in advance!

Play the [Ladder Lottery game](../assets/vis/amida-kuji.html). It draws one board for you to trace, and behind it draws two thousand more with the same number of rungs, so the histogram underneath is where your chosen line actually comes out. One knob sets the rungs; **Gap from even** is how far that histogram is from flat. Try to answer:

1. Suppose you knew you wanted to finish on line 7. With only four rungs on the board, is choosing where to start worth anything? Start at [four rungs](../assets/vis/amida-kuji.html?rungs=4) and look at the histogram.
2. Now drag the rungs up, and watch **Gap from even** fall: about 0.6 at four rungs, 0.3 at twenty, [0.08 at sixty](../assets/vis/amida-kuji.html?rungs=60). At what point does your choice of starting line stop being worth anything at all?

:::

The ladder is the smallest honest picture of what is coming. The vertical lines are the **states** the walker can occupy; the horizontal rungs are the **transitions** that move it from one state to the next. Where you land is decided by a rule you cannot see.

Be careful about *where* the randomness lives, because this is the one place the analogy could mislead you. A finished amida board is not random at all: it is a fixed permutation, and each starting line maps to exactly one ending line, every time. The uncertainty is in your ignorance of the board, not in your feet. What makes it a good rehearsal for random walks is the second question above: add more and more rungs, and the permutation the board induces becomes, from any starting line, as good as a uniform draw. Something unpredictable emerges from a pile of simple local rules. That emergence — and how many rungs it takes — is the subject of this module.

When we study random walks, four questions recur:

- **Short-term behavior**: where does the walker go in the first few steps?
- **Long-term behavior**: after many steps, where does it spend most of its time?
- **Structural insight**: what does the walker's behavior tell us about the network?
- **Applications**: how do we turn this into centrality and community detection?

Before going further, get the walk under your fingers. Open the [random walk simulator](../assets/vis/random-walks/index.html). **Walk** takes one step; **Run 5,000 steps** takes five thousand. The bar chart is the share of steps spent on each node, and the short mark across every bar is that node's $k/2m$ — the number this module is about to derive. **Distance to $k/2m$** is how far the whole chart still is from those marks. Answer these, first on the karate club network it loads by default, then on a [network with two obvious communities](../assets/vis/random-walks/index.html?dataFile=two-cliques.json):

1. Click **Walk** twenty times. Does the chart look like anything yet?
2. Now run five thousand steps, then five thousand more. Where does the walker spend most of its time, and how close do the bars get to their marks?
3. Does the behavior of the walker inform us about the centrality of the nodes?
4. On the two-community network, count how many consecutive steps the walker spends on one side before it crosses. Does the behavior of the walker inform us about communities?
5. Turn the teleport knob up to 0.3 and run it again. The distance stops falling and settles well above zero. What has the teleport done to the answer? (This is the same knob that turns a random walk into PageRank, in the centrality section below.)

## Why This Module Is the Hinge of the Course

Before the machinery, here is what one blind walker will buy us. Random walks are worth this much attention because they unify things we developed separately:

- **Centrality** (Module 6). PageRank *is* a random walk with teleportation; its stationary distribution is the ranking. Eigenvector centrality is what power iteration converges to, and power iteration is a walk. Degree centrality is the stationary distribution of the simple walk.
- **Community structure** (Module 5). Modularity is the difference between one-step and long-run co-location probabilities. Infomap and Walktrap define communities purely as regions where walks linger.
- **Distance**. Commute time and effective resistance give a notion of proximity that counts *all* routes rather than the shortest, often working better than shortest-path distance in practice.
- **Embedding** (Module 8). DeepWalk and node2vec turn walks into "sentences" and feed them to a language model. The embedding you get is determined by what the walk explores.
- **Spreading processes**. Diffusion and epidemic models are random walks with extra rules, so mixing time and spectral gap govern how fast a contagion spreads.

One process, five chapters. That is the payoff, and every term in that list is defined below.

## One Step: Divide by Your Degree

A random walk is characterized by the transition probabilities between nodes. The transition probability from node $i$ to node $j$ is:

$$
P_{ij} = \frac{A_{ij}}{k_i}
$$

where $A_{ij}$ is the adjacency matrix element and $k_i$ is the degree of node $i$. Read it as a sentence: *if there is an edge, split the walker's chance evenly among all $k_i$ of them; if there is no edge, the chance is zero.*

::: {#fig-m07-net}

![](../figs/m07-fig-01.svg){width=70%}

A ten-node network with thirteen edges. Node 1 has four neighbors (0, 2, 3, 4); node 7 has exactly one (node 2).

:::

Take node 1 in @fig-m07-net. It has four neighbors, so a walker standing on it moves to each of them with probability $1/4 = 0.25$, and to any of the other five nodes with probability $0$. Node 7 has a single neighbor, so a walker on node 7 moves to node 2 with probability $1$ — it has no choice at all. Every row of the matrix below is one such list of odds.

::: {#fig-m07-P}

![](../figs/m07-fig-02.svg){width=80%}

The transition matrix $\mathbf{P}$ of @fig-m07-net. Row $i$, column $j$ holds $P_{ij}$; each row sums to 1. Row 7 is a single 1 in column 2.

:::

Notice what the rule does *not* mention: how the walker arrived at node $i$. The next step depends only on where the walker is standing now, never on the route that brought it there. A process with this amnesia is called **Markovian**, and the amnesia itself is the **Markov property**. It is what lets us describe the entire future with one matrix.

Written for the whole network at once, "divide every row of $\mathbf{A}$ by that node's degree" is exactly

$$
\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{D}^{-1} \mathbf{A}
$$

where $\mathbf{D}$ is the diagonal matrix holding the degrees, $D_{ii} = k_i$. This one-line form is worth memorising — it is how the transition matrix is built in code, and it is the object we take apart spectrally later in the module.

We can represent all transition probabilities in a transition probability matrix $\mathbf{P}$:

$$
\mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix}
p_{11} & p_{12} & \cdots & p_{1N} \\
p_{21} & p_{22} & \cdots & p_{2N} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
p_{N1} & p_{N2} & \cdots & p_{NN}
\end{pmatrix}
$$

This matrix $\mathbf{P}$ encapsulates the entire random walk process. We can use it to calculate the probability of visiting each node after any number of steps:

- After one step: $P_{ij} = p_{ij}$
- After two steps: $\left(\mathbf{P}^{2}\right)_{ij} = \sum_{k} P_{ik} P_{kj}$
- After $T$ steps: $\left(\mathbf{P}^{T}\right)_{ij}$

Let's understand why $\mathbf{P}^2$ represents the transition probabilities after two steps.

First, recall that $\mathbf{P}_{ij}$ is the probability of moving from node $i$ to node $j$ in one step. Now, consider a two-step walk from $i$ to $j$. We can express this as:

$$
(\mathbf{P}^2)_{ij} = \sum_k \mathbf{P}_{ik} \mathbf{P}_{kj}
$$

This equation encapsulates a key idea: to go from $i$ to $j$ in two steps, we must pass through some intermediate node $k$. Let's break this down step by step:

1. The probability of the first step ($i$ to $k$) is $\mathbf{P}_{ik}$.
2. The probability of the second step ($k$ to $j$) is $\mathbf{P}_{kj}$.
3. The probability of this specific path ($i$ → $k$ → $j$) is the product $\mathbf{P}_{ik} \mathbf{P}_{kj}$.
4. We sum over all possible intermediate nodes $k$ to get the total probability.

And we can extend this reasoning for any number of steps $t$. In summary, for any number of steps $t$, $\left( \mathbf{P}^t \right)_{ij}$ gives the probability of being at node $j$ after $t$ steps, starting from node $i$.

## Where the Walker Ends Up: Degree, and Nothing Else

The **stationary distribution** is the probability distribution of the walker after infinitely many steps — the long-term behavior of the walker.

Assume for the moment that such a distribution exists. (For an undirected network it does, provided two conditions hold; we state them below, because both fail in networks you will actually meet.) At the stationary state the walker must satisfy the balance condition

$$
x(t+1) = x(t) \; \text{for a large } t,
$$

where $x(t)$ is the probability distribution of the walker at time $t$. We write it as a **row** vector,

$$
x(t) = \begin{pmatrix} x_1(t) & x_2(t) & \cdots & x_N(t) \end{pmatrix}
$$

with $x_i(t)$ the probability of being at node $i$ at time $t$, and $\sum_i x_i(t) = 1$. Writing it as a row is a convenience, not a deep choice: it lets one step of the walk be multiplication on the right by $\mathbf{P}$, so the formula reads left to right in the order things happen. The balance condition means the system has become time invariant: the probability of being at node $i$ is the same at time $t$ and at time $t+1$.

What does $x(t)$ look like in the stationary state? Represent $x(t)$ using $\mathbf{P}$ and an initial distribution $x(0)$:

$$
x(t) = x(t-1)\,\mathbf{P} = x(0)\,\mathbf{P}^t .
$$

So the question becomes: what does $\mathbf{P}^t$ look like for large $t$?

Take the matrix apart before doing any algebra. Row $i$ of $\mathbf{P}^t$ is
one walker's whole future: it lists where a walker that started at node $i$
might be $t$ steps later. Below, every entry is drawn as a square of ink —
darker for likelier — so a row is a stripe you can read at a glance. Step
through the first three powers one at a time, then drag $t$ and watch what
becomes of the rows.

```{=html}
    /* t=20 */ [[79,158,119,156,157,115,71,40,71,33],[79,158,119,157,157,115,71,40,71,33],[79,159,120,157,157,115,70,40,70,32],[78,157,118,157,157,112,78,40,66,38],[78,157,118,157,157,112,78,40,65,38],[77,154,115,149,149,127,62,38,101,28],[71,141,104,155,155,93,124,36,45,75],[80,160,120,158,159,113,72,41,64,34],[71,142,105,132,131,152,45,32,173,17],[66,132,96,154,153,83,151,34,34,97]],
    /* t=25 */ [[78,156,117,156,156,114,75,39,72,37],[78,156,117,156,156,114,75,39,72,37],[78,156,118,156,156,114,75,39,71,37],[78,156,117,154,154,117,73,39,78,35],[78,156,117,154,154,117,72,39,78,35],[76,152,114,156,156,109,88,39,64,47],[75,151,113,145,145,132,60,36,117,26],[78,157,118,156,156,116,72,39,73,35],[72,143,106,155,155,96,117,37,48,70],[74,147,110,140,139,141,53,35,141,22]],
    /* t=32 */ [[77,155,116,154,154,116,75,39,76,37],[77,155,116,154,154,115,75,39,76,37],[77,155,116,154,154,116,75,39,76,37],[77,154,116,155,155,114,78,39,74,39],[77,154,116,155,155,114,78,39,74,39],[77,154,116,152,152,119,72,38,85,35],[75,151,113,155,155,108,91,38,64,50],[77,155,116,155,155,115,76,39,74,38],[76,152,114,148,148,127,64,37,105,29],[74,149,111,155,155,104,99,38,59,56]],
    /* t=40 */ [[77,154,116,154,154,115,76,39,77,38],[77,154,116,154,154,115,76,39,77,38],[77,154,116,154,154,115,76,39,77,38],[77,154,116,154,154,115,77,39,76,39],[77,154,116,154,154,115,77,39,76,39],[77,154,115,153,153,117,74,38,81,37],[76,153,114,155,155,112,83,38,70,43],[77,154,116,154,154,115,77,39,76,38],[77,153,115,151,151,121,70,38,90,34],[76,152,114,155,155,110,87,38,67,46]],
    /* t=50 */ [[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,76,39],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,76,39],[77,154,115,154,154,116,76,38,78,38],[77,153,115,154,154,114,79,38,74,40],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,39,77,38],[77,154,115,153,153,118,74,38,82,36],[77,153,115,154,154,113,81,38,73,41]],
    /* t=65 */ [[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,39],[77,154,115,154,154,116,76,38,78,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,78,38,76,39],[77,154,115,154,154,116,76,38,78,38]],
    /* t=80 */ [[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,39],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,116,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,39]],
    /* t=100 */ [[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38],[77,154,115,154,154,115,77,38,77,38]]
  ];

  const DET = [1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,13,16,20,25,32,40,50,65,80,100];
  const SPREAD = [1.0000,0.7500,0.7500,0.6042,0.6042,0.4983,0.4142,0.3452,0.2820,0.2001,0.1390,0.0921,0.0465,0.0223,0.0089,0.0023,0.0006,0.0001];
  const L2T = [0.91196,0.83167,0.75845,0.69168,0.63079,0.57525,0.47842,0.39789,0.30178,0.22889,0.15832,0.09987,0.05239,0.02506,0.00997,0.00250,0.00063,0.00010];

  const DEG = [2,4,3,4,4,3,2,1,2,1];
  const TWO_M = 26;
  const PI = DEG.map((k) => k / TWO_M);
  const NL = 10;

  /* ------------------------------------------------------------- geometry --- */
  const CELL = 13, GX0 = 30, GY0 = 26;    /* the heatmap */
  const PX = (i) => 41 + 22 * i;          /* centre of column i's bar pair */
  const PYB = 96, PPLOT = 74, PAXIS = 0.35;
  const f3 = (x) => x.toFixed(3);
  const f2 = (x) => x.toFixed(2);
  /* Ink density. Straight opacity would draw the settled matrix — every entry
     around 0.1 — as a blank sheet, so the square root is taken first. It is a
     monotone re-inking, not a recolouring: darker still means likelier, and
     the caption says so. */
  const dens = (v) => Math.sqrt(v);

  /* --------------------------------------------------------------- scenes --- */
  const scenes = [
    {
      label: "Each row is a starting node",
      note: "The transition matrix drawn as ink: row i is a walker that started at node i, column j is where it might be one step later. Row 7 is a single black square — a walker on node 7 has nowhere to go but node 2. Row 1 is four grey squares of a quarter each.",
      async run(ctx) {
        ctx.build();
        ctx.dial(0);
        ctx.highlight(true);
        const c = ctx.say("two rows, one step in");
        [["row 7, the leaf", "node 2, certain"],
         ["row 1, the hub", "four nodes, &frac14; each"]].forEach((row, i) => {
          const t = ctx.el("div", "anim-tally anim-fade",
            "<span>" + row[0] + "</span><b>" + row[1] + "</b>");
          t.style.animationDelay = ctx.fast() ? "0s" : (0.8 + i * 0.6) + "s";
          c.appendChild(t);
        });
        if (!ctx.fast()) await ctx.sleep(2400);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-quote anim-fade",
          "nothing the two rows do is alike. The widest gap between them is a " +
          "whole unit of probability, in column 2."));
        await ctx.sleep(3200);
      }
    },
    {
      label: "Two steps, then three",
      note: "Take a second step, then a third. Every dark square bleeds into its neighbours' neighbours; the diagonal fills in, because two steps can bring the walker home. The widest disagreement between two rows drops from 1.000 to 0.750.",
      async run(ctx) {
        const c = ctx.say("what a second step does");
        if (!ctx.fast()) await ctx.sleep(600);
        ctx.dial(1);
        if (!ctx.fast()) await ctx.sleep(1600);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-tally anim-fade",
          "<span>diagonal at t = 2</span><b>never zero</b>"));
        if (!ctx.fast()) await ctx.sleep(1400);
        ctx.dial(2);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-tally anim-fade",
          "<span>rows differ by</span><b>1.000 &rarr; 0.750</b>"));
        if (!ctx.fast()) await ctx.sleep(1600);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-quote anim-fade",
          "three steps in, the leaf-walker is still nothing like the " +
          "hub-walker. But the black square is gone: certainty was the first " +
          "thing to go."));
        await ctx.sleep(3200);
      }
    },
    {
      label: "Watch the rows fall together",
      note: "Now run t up to a hundred. The scatter turns into vertical stripes: inside a column every row ends the same shade. The stripe darkness is k over 2m, and the dashed markers show the two profiles landing on it.",
      async run(ctx) {
        const c = ctx.say("t climbing to a hundred");
        const big = ctx.el("div", "anim-big", "3");
        c.appendChild(big);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption", "steps"));
        const verdict = ctx.el("div", "anim-tally anim-fade");
        verdict.style.visibility = "hidden";
        c.appendChild(verdict);

        if (ctx.fast()) {
          ctx.dial(DET.length - 1);
          ctx.marks(true);
          big.textContent = "100";
          verdict.innerHTML = "<span>every row</span><b>the same row</b>";
          verdict.style.visibility = "visible";
          return;
        }

        for (let i = 3; i < DET.length; i++) {
          ctx.dial(i);
          big.textContent = String(DET[i]);
          await ctx.sleep(i < 10 ? 620 : 480);
        }
        verdict.innerHTML = "<span>every row</span><b>the same row</b>";
        verdict.style.visibility = "visible";
        await ctx.sleep(1400);
        ctx.marks(true);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-quote anim-fade",
          "the columns still differ &mdash; that is the degree sequence, " +
          "k/2m. What went away is any difference <em>between rows</em>: the " +
          "walker no longer carries where it came from."));
        await ctx.sleep(3800);
      }
    },
    {
      label: "Now you turn it",
      note: "Drag t yourself and watch the readout. At t = 20 two rows can still disagree by 0.139; by t = 65 the widest disagreement is down to 0.002, and by t = 100 every row is the identical row to three decimals. How far you must drag before that happens is the mixing time.",
      async run(ctx) {
        const c = ctx.say("you turn it");
        ctx.marks(true);
        const track = ctx.el("div", "anim-track");
        const knob = ctx.el("div", "anim-knob");
        track.appendChild(knob);
        c.appendChild(track);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption",
          "drag: t runs from one step to a hundred"));

        [["t = 3", "rows differ by 0.750"],
         ["t = 20", "rows differ by 0.139"],
         ["t = 65", "rows differ by 0.002"]].forEach((row, i) => {
          const t = ctx.el("div", "anim-tally anim-fade",
            "<span>" + row[0] + "</span><b>" + row[1] + "</b>");
          t.style.animationDelay = ctx.fast() ? "0s" : (0.5 + i * 0.5) + "s";
          c.appendChild(t);
        });

        const dial = ctx.mountKnob(knob, {
          min: 0, max: DET.length - 1, step: 1, value: DET.length - 1,
          label: "Number of steps t",
          format: (i) => "t = " + DET[i],
          onGrab: () => ctx.pause(),
          onInput: (i) => ctx.dial(i)
        });

        if (ctx.fast()) { dial.set(DET.length - 1); return; }

        /* Park on the last detent, then sweep back to one and up again once,
           so it is obvious the knob goes both ways before the reader takes it. */
        dial.set(DET.length - 1);
        await ctx.sleep(2600);
        for (let i = DET.length - 2; i >= 0; i--) { dial.set(i); await ctx.sleep(150); }
        await ctx.sleep(900);
        c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-quote anim-fade",
          "every extra step multiplies whatever disagreement is left by about " +
          "0.912 &mdash; the second largest eigenvalue of <b>P</b>. That one " +
          "number is the whole clock, and the next section is about nothing else."));
        for (let i = 1; i < DET.length; i++) { dial.set(i); await ctx.sleep(150); }
        await ctx.sleep(4200);
      }
    }
  ];

  mountScenes(document.getElementById("rw-forget"), scenes, {
    stepsLabel: "Matrix powers",

    /* The two things only this animation has: a 10x10 grid of ink and a pair
       of row profiles beside it. Both are built once, in scene 1, and only
       re-inked afterwards — so jumping to a step still lands on a drawing,
       because the kit fast-forwards the earlier scenes first. */
    helpers(ctx) {
      const gridBox = ctx.$("[data-rf-grid]");
      const profBox = ctx.$("[data-rf-prof]");
      const side = ctx.$("[data-rf-say]");
      const S = { at: 0 };

      /* ---------------------------------------------------------- the build */
      function build() {
        gridBox.textContent = "";
        profBox.textContent = "";
        const slow = !ctx.fast();

        /* ---- the heatmap ---- */
        const svg = ctx.svgRoot("0 0 176 176");
        const gCell = svg.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("g"));
        const gHl = svg.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("g"));
        const gLab = svg.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("g"));

        S.cell = [];
        for (let r = 0; r < NL; r++) {
          const row = [];
          for (let c = 0; c < NL; c++) {
            const q = ctx.svgEl("rect", {
              x: GX0 + c * CELL, y: GY0 + r * CELL,
              width: CELL, height: CELL, "class": "rf-cell"
            });
            q.style.fillOpacity = 0;
            if (slow) {
              q.classList.add("anim-fade");
              q.style.animationDelay = (0.05 + (r + c) * 0.03) + "s";
            }
            row.push(gCell.appendChild(q));
          }
          S.cell.push(row);
        }

        S.hl = [1, 7].map((r, j) => {
          const q = ctx.svgEl("rect", {
            x: GX0 - 1.5, y: GY0 + r * CELL - 1.5,
            width: NL * CELL + 3, height: CELL + 3,
            "class": "rf-hl " + (j === 0 ? "rf-hl-a" : "rf-hl-b")
          });
          q.style.opacity = 0;
          return gHl.appendChild(q);
        });

        for (let i = 0; i < NL; i++) {
          const ct = ctx.svgEl("text",
            { x: GX0 + i * CELL + CELL / 2, y: GY0 - 5, "class": "rf-num" });
          ct.textContent = String(i);
          gLab.appendChild(ct);
          const rt = ctx.svgEl("text",
            { x: GX0 - 5, y: GY0 + i * CELL + CELL / 2 + 3.2, "class": "rf-num rf-end" });
          rt.textContent = String(i);
          gLab.appendChild(rt);
        }
        const to = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: GX0 + NL * CELL / 2, y: 12, "class": "rf-side" });
        to.textContent = "to →";
        to.setAttribute("text-anchor", "middle");
        gLab.appendChild(to);
        const from = ctx.svgEl("text", {
          x: 11, y: GY0 + NL * CELL / 2, "class": "rf-side",
          transform: "rotate(-90 11 " + (GY0 + NL * CELL / 2) + ")"
        });
        from.textContent = "started at ↓";
        from.setAttribute("text-anchor", "middle");
        gLab.appendChild(from);

        gridBox.appendChild(svg);

        S.read = ctx.el("div", "anim-readout anim-readout--tight",
          '<span>t <b data-t>1</b></span>' +
          '<span>rows differ by <b data-s>1.000</b></span>' +
          '<span>&lambda;<sub>2</sub><sup>t</sup> <b data-l>0.912</b></span>');
        gridBox.appendChild(S.read);
        S.outT = S.read.querySelector("[data-t]");
        S.outS = S.read.querySelector("[data-s]");
        S.outL = S.read.querySelector("[data-l]");

        gridBox.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption",
          "one square per entry of <b>P</b><sup>t</sup>; darker means likelier. " +
          "Darkness is the square root of the probability, so the small entries " +
          "are still visible &mdash; nothing but density, no colour scale."));

        /* ---- the two row profiles ---- */
        const psvg = ctx.svgRoot("0 0 260 124");
        const gBar = psvg.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("g"));
        const gMark = psvg.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("g"));
        const gAx = psvg.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("g"));

        S.b1 = []; S.b7 = []; S.over = [];
        for (let i = 0; i < NL; i++) {
          S.b1.push(gBar.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("rect", {
            x: PX(i) - 9, y: PYB, width: 8, height: 0, "class": "anim-accent-fill"
          })));
          S.b7.push(gBar.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("rect", {
            x: PX(i) + 1, y: PYB, width: 8, height: 0, "class": "anim-amber-fill"
          })));
          const o = ctx.svgEl("text",
            { x: PX(i), y: PYB - PPLOT - 3, "class": "rf-over" });
          S.over.push(gAx.appendChild(o));
        }

        S.mark = [];
        for (let i = 0; i < NL; i++) {
          const y = PYB - (Math.min(PI[i], PAXIS) / PAXIS) * PPLOT;
          const l = ctx.svgEl("line", {
            x1: PX(i) - 14, x2: PX(i) + 14, y1: y, y2: y,
            "class": "anim-marker anim-marker--faint"
          });
          l.style.opacity = 0;
          S.mark.push(gMark.appendChild(l));
        }

        gAx.appendChild(ctx.svgEl("line",
          { x1: 26, y1: PYB, x2: 256, y2: PYB, "class": "anim-axis" }));
        const top = ctx.svgEl("text",
          { x: 22, y: PYB - PPLOT + 4, "class": "rf-num rf-end" });
        top.textContent = "0.35";
        gAx.appendChild(top);
        const zero = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: 22, y: PYB + 4, "class": "rf-num rf-end" });
        zero.textContent = "0";
        gAx.appendChild(zero);
        for (let i = 0; i < NL; i++) {
          const n = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: PX(i), y: PYB + 14, "class": "rf-num" });
          n.textContent = String(i);
          gAx.appendChild(n);
          const d = ctx.svgEl("text", { x: PX(i), y: PYB + 25, "class": "rf-num rf-dim" });
          d.textContent = "k=" + DEG[i];
          gAx.appendChild(d);
        }

        profBox.appendChild(psvg);
        profBox.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption",
          'the two outlined rows, side by side: ' +
          '<span style="color:var(--_accent)">&#9632;</span> row 1 (started at the hub) ' +
          'and <span style="color:var(--_amber)">&#9632;</span> row 7 (started at the leaf). ' +
          'The dashed markers, once they appear, sit at k/2m.'));

        paint(0);
      }

      /* Everything both drawings show at detent d. Pure lookup: no arithmetic
         on the matrix, only on where to put the ink. */
      function paint(d) {
        S.at = d;
        const M = PT[d];
        for (let r = 0; r < NL; r++) {
          for (let c = 0; c < NL; c++) {
            S.cell[r][c].style.fillOpacity = dens(M[r][c] / 1000).toFixed(3);
          }
        }
        const r1 = M[1], r7 = M[7];
        for (let i = 0; i < NL; i++) {
          const v1 = r1[i] / 1000, v7 = r7[i] / 1000;
          const h1 = (Math.min(v1, PAXIS) / PAXIS) * PPLOT;
          const h7 = (Math.min(v7, PAXIS) / PAXIS) * PPLOT;
          ctx.attr(S.b1[i], { y: PYB - h1, height: h1 });
          ctx.attr(S.b7[i], { y: PYB - h7, height: h7 });
          const big = Math.max(v1, v7);
          if (big > PAXIS) {
            S.over[i].textContent = f2(big);
            S.over[i].setAttribute("fill",
              v7 >= v1 ? "var(--_amber)" : "var(--_accent)");
          } else {
            S.over[i].textContent = "";
          }
        }
        S.outT.textContent = String(DET[d]);
        S.outS.textContent = f3(SPREAD[d]);
        S.outL.textContent = f3(L2T[d]);
      }

      function say(title) {
        side.textContent = "";
        const c = ctx.el("div", "anim-panel anim-pop");
        if (title) c.appendChild(ctx.el("div", "anim-caption", title));
        side.appendChild(c);
        return c;
      }

      /* S is filled by build(), i.e. after helpers() has already run, so
         everything reaching into it has to be a function — the kit copies
         these onto ctx by value at mount time. */
      return {
        build: build,
        say: say,
        dial: paint,
        marks: function (on) {
          S.mark.forEach((l) => { l.style.opacity = on ? 1 : 0; });
        },
        highlight: function (on) {
          S.hl.forEach((q) => { q.style.opacity = on ? 1 : 0; });
        }
      };
    }
  });
});
</script>
```

The last frame of that widget, written out as numbers, is @fig-long-term-P.

::: {#fig-long-term-P}

![](../figs/long-term-P.svg){width=80%}

$\mathbf{P}^{100}$ for the network in @fig-m07-net. Every row is identical: after a hundred steps it no longer matters where the walker started.

:::

Compare it with @fig-m07-P, where no two rows had anything in common. That is the whole phenomenon in one picture: after enough steps, the walker's position no longer carries any trace of where it began. Note what did *not* disappear. The columns of @fig-long-term-P are still unequal — column 1 is four times column 7 — and that surviving difference is the answer to the question the next section asks.

Why does $\mathbf{P}^t$ have this peculiar property? Because of the spectral properties of $\mathbf{P}$. We can rewrite the balance condition as an eigenvalue equation:

$$
\pi = \pi \mathbf{P}
$$

where $\pi=\lim_{t\to\infty} x(t)$ is the stationary distribution. So $\pi$ is parallel to a left eigenvector of $\mathbf{P}$.

::: {.column-margin}
$\pi$ is *parallel* to that left eigenvector, not equal to it. An eigenvector has no canonical length — any multiple of it is still an eigenvector — and numerical libraries happen to hand you the one of unit Euclidean length. We want the multiple whose entries sum to 1, so rescale by dividing through by the sum.
:::

That left eigenvector is the one associated with the largest eigenvalue of $\mathbf{P}$, as per the Perron–Frobenius theorem. The intuition is conservation: the number of walkers in a graph is unchanged by a transition, which is evident from $\sum_{j} P_{ij}=1$ (if the row sum were greater than 1, walkers would multiply and explode to infinity). In the language of spectra, nothing is rescaled, and that corresponds to an eigenvalue of exactly 1 — visible as the topmost point in @fig-spectrum.

::: {.column-margin}

![Spectrum of the transition matrix $\mathbf{P}$ for @fig-m07-net. One eigenvalue sits at exactly 1; the rest are strictly smaller in magnitude.](../figs/spectrum.svg){#fig-spectrum}

:::

The other eigenvalues are less than one in magnitude and describe the short-term behavior of the walk, which is the subject of the next section.

### The Answer Is the Degree Sequence

Calling $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ "the leading left eigenvector" describes it but does not tell you what it *is*. For an undirected network the answer is startlingly simple, and you can guess it before proving it.

Feel it first. The walker never chooses a node — it chooses an **edge**. So a node with twice as many edges catches the walker roughly twice as often. That is the whole idea:

$$
\pi_i \propto k_i.
$$

To turn the proportionality into an equality, the probabilities must sum to one. Every edge contributes 2 to the total degree (one at each end), so $\sum_i k_i = 2m$ for a network with $m$ edges — the handshake count from Module 1. Dividing by that total gives

::: {.callout-important title="The stationary distribution of a simple random walk"}
$$
\pi_i = \frac{k_i}{\sum_\ell k_\ell} = \frac{k_i}{2m}
$$

In the long run, the fraction of time the walker spends at a node is its share of the edge endpoints in the network. Nothing else about the structure survives.
:::

Put numbers on it with @fig-m07-net, which has $m = 13$ edges and therefore $2m = 26$ edge endpoints. Node 1, with $k_1 = 4$, gets $\pi_1 = 4/26 \approx 0.154$; node 7, with $k_7 = 1$, gets $\pi_7 = 1/26 \approx 0.038$. Rounded to two decimals, $0.15$ and $0.04$ are exactly the numbers printed in every row of @fig-long-term-P — and they are the two markers the walker's bars landed on at the top of this page.

Checking the guess takes one line. Substitute it into the balance condition $\boldsymbol{\pi} = \boldsymbol{\pi} \mathbf{P}$:

$$
\left(\boldsymbol{\pi}\mathbf{P}\right)_j
= \sum_i \pi_i P_{ij}
= \sum_i \frac{k_i}{2m}\cdot\frac{A_{ij}}{k_i}
= \frac{1}{2m}\sum_i A_{ij}
= \frac{k_j}{2m}
= \pi_j .
$$

The degrees cancel, which is the whole trick: the $k_i$ that makes a hub attractive is the same $k_i$ that thins out each of its outgoing steps.

::: {.column-margin}
Two consequences to carry forward. First, the stationary distribution of a simple walk on an undirected network *is* degree centrality, rescaled — which is why Module 6's walk-based measures needed teleportation to say anything new. Second, this holds only for undirected networks; on a directed network $\pi_i \propto k_i$ is false, and PageRank exists precisely to supply a well-behaved substitute.
:::

### When a Stationary Distribution Fails to Exist

We assumed above that a stationary distribution exists. Two conditions make that assumption safe, and both fail in networks you will actually meet.

**Irreducibility.** The walker must be able to reach every node from every node. If the network is disconnected, a walker starting in one component never visits the others, and there is no single stationary distribution — there is one per component. This is why we usually extract the giant component (Module 1) before doing anything.

**Aperiodicity.** The walker must not be trapped in a rigid rhythm. Consider a **bipartite** network — nodes split into two sides, edges only between sides. A walker starting on the left is on the right after one step, back on the left after two, and so on forever. The distribution oscillates with period 2 and never settles, even though the network is perfectly connected.

A random walk with both properties is called **ergodic**, and only then are we guaranteed a unique stationary distribution reached from *any* starting point. The fix for periodicity is easy: add a small chance of staying put (a "lazy" walk), or add teleportation as PageRank does. Either one destroys the rigid alternation.

You can see both conditions in the spectrum. Disconnection shows up as eigenvalue 1 appearing more than once — one copy per component. Periodicity shows up as an eigenvalue at exactly $-1$, the mode that flips sign at every step and therefore never decays.

### A Walk Looks the Same Played Backwards

Undirected random walks have a symmetry that makes much of the theory work. In the stationary state, the probability of being at $i$ and stepping to $j$ equals the probability of being at $j$ and stepping to $i$:

$$
\pi_i P_{ij} = \frac{k_i}{2m}\cdot\frac{A_{ij}}{k_i} = \frac{A_{ij}}{2m} = \frac{k_j}{2m}\cdot\frac{A_{ji}}{k_j} = \pi_j P_{ji}
$$

This is called **detailed balance**, and a walk satisfying it is **reversible**: a recording of the walk played backwards is statistically indistinguishable from one played forwards.

Reversibility is what lets us symmetrize $\mathbf{P}$ in the next section — the trick that makes the spectral analysis possible at all. Random walks on *directed* networks are generally not reversible, which is exactly why they are harder.

## How Long Until the Walker Forgets Where It Started?

The stationary distribution says where the walker ends up. It says nothing about *when*. Drop a walker on a ring of 1000 nodes and it takes on the order of a million steps before its position is anywhere close to uniform. Drop it on the karate club and a dozen steps will do. Same kind of destination, wildly different waiting time.

Feel it first. Start one walker at node 1 and another at node 7. At $t = 1$ their distributions are completely different — one is spread over four neighbors, the other sits on node 2 with certainty. At every step the difference shrinks a little. **Mixing time** is how long you must wait before that difference drops below a tolerance $\epsilon$ you are willing to accept: the moment when knowing the starting node tells you essentially nothing about where the walker is now.

$$
t_{\text{mix}} = \min\left\{t : \max_{x(0)} \|x(t) - \boldsymbol{\pi}\|_{1} \leq \epsilon\right\}
$$

The picture that explains the answer is @fig-long-term-P again: mixing time is how many powers of $\mathbf{P}$ you must take before the rows become indistinguishable.

One number controls it. The gap between the walker's distribution and $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ can be split into modes, one per eigenvalue of $\mathbf{P}$, and each step multiplies mode $\ell$ by its eigenvalue $\lambda_\ell$. The largest eigenvalue is $\lambda_1 = 1$: that mode *is* $\boldsymbol{\pi}$, and it never decays. Every other mode shrinks, and the slowest of them is the second largest, $\lambda_2$. After $t$ steps the leftover error is of size $\lambda_2^{\,t}$, so the whole clock is set by how far $\lambda_2$ sits below 1. (Strictly it is the largest eigenvalue in *magnitude* other than 1 that matters: a mode at $-1$ flips sign instead of decaying, which is the periodicity problem from the previous section.)

That distance has a name. The **spectral gap** is $1 - \lambda_2$, and its reciprocal

$$
\tau = \frac{1}{1 - \lambda_2}
$$

is the **relaxation time** — the number of steps in which the slowest mode shrinks by a factor of $e$. Mixing time is the relaxation time multiplied by a logarithmic factor that pays for how small a tolerance $\epsilon$ you demanded and how rare the rarest node is:

$$
t_{\text{mix}} < \frac{1}{1-\lambda_2} \log \left( \frac{1}{\epsilon \, \min_{i} \pi_i} \right)
= \tau \log \left( \frac{1}{\epsilon \, \min_{i} \pi_i} \right)
$$

Read that carefully: $\tau$ on its own is *not* a bound on $t_{\text{mix}}$. It is a time *scale* — mixing takes a few $\tau$'s, and the logarithm says how many. Demand a tighter $\epsilon$, or add a node so rare that $\pi_i$ is tiny, and you pay for it inside the logarithm.

::: {.column-margin}
The same quantity is often written with the normalized Laplacian, whose second smallest eigenvalue is $\mu = 1 - \lambda_2$, giving $\tau = 1/\mu$. That is the same $\mu$ Module 5's spectral clustering minimises, which is why "good cut" and "slow mixing" turn out to be the same statement.
:::

A worked number. Take two 5-cliques joined by a single edge — ten nodes, one obvious bottleneck. Its transition matrix has $\lambda_2 = 0.927$, so the spectral gap is $0.073$ and $\tau \approx 14$ steps. Now merge the two cliques into one 10-clique, keeping the same ten nodes: $\lambda_2 = -1/9$, the gap is $1.11$, and $\tau \approx 0.9$ steps — a single step essentially finishes the job. Same node count, a fifteen-fold difference in mixing, and the only thing that changed is a bottleneck. Hold on to this: it is the reason random walks can find communities at all.

Why the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{P}$ govern $\mathbf{P}^t$ at all — and the trick that makes a non-symmetric $\mathbf{P}$ behave like a symmetric one — is worked out in the [appendix](04-appendix.qmd), which also shows the leading mode reproducing $\pi_i = k_i/2m$ on its own.

## Return, Hit, Commute, Cover: Four Clocks on a Walk

The stationary distribution answers "where does the walker end up in the long run?" and mixing time answers "how long until we can stop caring where it started?". A third family of questions is about *specific* trips, and it gives us a set of distance-like quantities that are often more useful than shortest paths.

### Return Time

Start at node $i$ and walk until you come back. How long does that take on average?

The answer follows from the stationary distribution with no extra work. If the walker spends a fraction $\pi_i$ of its time at node $i$, then it visits $i$ once every $1/\pi_i$ steps on average:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{return time to } i] = \frac{1}{\pi_i} = \frac{2m}{k_i}
$$

In @fig-m07-net, node 1 is revisited every $26/4 = 6.5$ steps on average, while node 7 waits $26/1 = 26$ steps. At larger scale: a hub with $k_i = 100$ in a network with $m = 1000$ edges is revisited every 20 steps; a leaf with $k_i = 1$ waits 2000 steps.

### Hitting Time and Commute Time

The **hitting time** $h_{ij}$ is the expected number of steps to reach $j$ for the first time, starting from $i$.

The crucial and surprising property is that **hitting time is not symmetric**: $h_{ij} \neq h_{ji}$ in general. Walking from a leaf to a hub is quick — most steps lead toward well-connected regions. Walking from the hub back to that specific leaf takes far longer, because the hub has a hundred other places to go. Asymmetry is not a defect; it reflects a real feature of the network that shortest-path distance, which is always symmetric, cannot express.

If you want symmetry, take the round trip. The **commute time** is

$$
C_{ij} = h_{ij} + h_{ji}
$$

which *is* symmetric and behaves much more like a distance. Two nodes have small commute time when they are connected by *many* short routes, not merely one — so unlike shortest-path distance, commute time rewards redundancy of connection.

Replace every edge with a 1-ohm resistor and the analogy becomes exact: commute time is proportional to the **effective resistance** $R_{ij}$ between the two nodes, $C_{ij} = 2m \cdot R_{ij}$. Resistors in parallel reduce resistance, which is the electrical statement of "many routes make nodes close". This correspondence lets you import a century of circuit theory into network analysis, and it explains why commute time is a better similarity measure than shortest path for recommendation and link prediction.

### Cover Time

The **cover time** is the expected number of steps to visit *every* node at least once. It matters whenever a walk is being used to explore or sample an unknown network — crawling the web, sampling users of a social platform — because it bounds how long you must run before you can hope to have seen everything. Cover time grows roughly like $N \log N$ on well-connected networks and much worse on networks with bottlenecks.

## Five Ways to Change the Rules

The simple random walk — uniform choice among neighbors — is a starting point, not the only option. Each variant below changes the transition probabilities and therefore changes what the walk reveals.

**Biased random walks.** Instead of choosing uniformly, weight the choice. A degree-biased walk favors (or avoids) high-degree neighbors; the stationary distribution shifts accordingly, and you can even design a bias that makes it *uniform*, which is useful for unbiased sampling. An attribute-biased walk prefers neighbors similar to the current node.

**Random walk with restart (teleportation).** At each step, with probability $\alpha$ jump back to the starting node instead of following an edge. This keeps the walk near its origin, and its stationary distribution is a measure of proximity to that origin. You have already seen this: it is personalized PageRank from Module 6, viewed as a process rather than an equation.

**Second-order walks.** Let the next step depend on the *previous* node as well as the current one, so the walker can be discouraged from backtracking or encouraged to stay local. This breaks the Markov property in the node state — the next step now depends on history, not only on the current position — and it is exactly the machinery node2vec uses in Module 8.

**Self-avoiding walks.** Forbid revisiting any node. This sounds like a small change but is a much harder object: the walker can get stuck with nowhere to go, and the process is not Markovian at all. Self-avoiding walks are important in polymer physics and in certain sampling algorithms.

**Walks on directed networks.** Transition probabilities become asymmetric, $\pi_i \propto k_i$ no longer holds, and the walk can reach a **dead end** — a node with no outgoing edges — where it simply stops. Teleportation is the standard remedy, which is precisely why PageRank needs it.

## When Nobody Knows the Shortest Path

If the stationary distribution ranks nodes by how often a walker visits them, it is already a centrality — and for undirected networks it is just degree centrality in disguise, since $\pi_i \propto k_i$. Walk-based thinking becomes genuinely new when we look at *trajectories* rather than the endpoint.

**Random walk betweenness.** Shortest-path betweenness (Module 6) assumes that whatever flows through the network knows the optimal route. Rumors, money and infections do not. Random walk betweenness instead counts how often a random walk from $s$ to $t$ passes through node $i$, averaged over all pairs $(s,t)$. Nodes that lie on many *plausible* routes score highly, even when they are on no shortest path at all. It is also more stable: adding one edge can reroute many shortest paths at once, but it barely perturbs a diffusive flow.

**Random walk closeness.** Replace shortest-path distance with expected hitting time and you get a closeness measure that accounts for the number of routes, not just the shortest one.

::: {.column-margin}
The pattern is general and worth remembering: for almost every shortest-path-based quantity there is a random-walk counterpart. The shortest-path version asks "what is the best route?"; the random-walk version asks "what happens if nobody knows the best route?" Which one you want depends entirely on what is flowing.
:::

## Communities Are Where the Walker Gets Stuck

Random walks reveal community structure because of the worked number above. Before reaching the steady state, a walker tends to remain within its starting community and only gradually leaks into the others.

Take that literally and watch it happen. Below are the two joined cliques from
the mixing-time section, with seven nodes on each side instead of five — which
only deepens the trap, $\tau = 27$ steps rather than 14. Follow one walker step
by step, and at the same time watch a crowd of a hundred walkers released with
it drain out of the room they all started in. Then open more doors and see what
changes.
